words.definition: Able to be changed or altered over time.
words.example: Software settings are mutable, so you can adjust them whenever your needs shift.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'mutare' (to change) — the same root as 'mutation,' which rewrites DNA.

words.definition: Fixed and impossible to alter in any way.
words.example: The laws of physics are immutable, holding true no matter what we wish.
words.mnemonic: im- (not) + 'mutable' — picture an immovable stone monument that never shifts.

words.definition: Lasting only a brief moment before disappearing.
words.example: The mayfly's ephemeral life spans barely a single day.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'epi-hemera' = upon a day; mayflies (order Ephemeroptera) live about one day.

words.definition: Staying or existing for only a short period.
words.example: The motel catered to transient guests who rarely stayed more than one night.
words.mnemonic: Shares its root with 'transit' — a transient is just passing through, like traffic in transit.

words.definition: Not lasting; soon passing away.
words.example: Fame proved transitory for the singer, fading within a single season.
words.mnemonic: Also built on 'transit' — plus -tory, like a story that ends as soon as it begins.

words.definition: Passing very quickly and gone in an instant.
words.example: She caught only a fleeting glimpse of the deer before it bolted into the trees.
words.mnemonic: A fleet moves fast, and a fleeting moment flees before you can hold it.

words.definition: Quickly fading from sight or memory.
words.example: The evanescent morning mist burned away the moment the sun rose over the hills.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'vanish' inside it — evaneSCENT, a scent that vanishes into thin air.

words.definition: Continuing or recurring year after year.
words.example: Traffic congestion is a perennial complaint that returns every summer.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'per-annus' = through the years; perennial plants bloom every year (per-annual).

words.definition: Continuing forever without interruption.
words.example: The waterfall's perpetual roar never quieted, day or night.
words.mnemonic: Think of a perpetual-motion machine — the fantasy device that supposedly never stops.

words.definition: Lasting over a long period despite hardship or difficulty.
words.example: Their friendship proved enduring, surviving decades apart and half a world of distance.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'durare' (to harden, to last) — the same root as 'durable' steel.

words.definition: Continuing steadily for a long time without fading.
words.example: He had an abiding love of the sea that stayed with him all his life.
words.mnemonic: To 'abide' is to stay or dwell — an abiding guest is the one who never leaves.

words.definition: Impossible to stop, prevent, or persuade against.
words.example: The inexorable advance of the glacier crushed everything in its path.
words.mnemonic: in- (not) + 'exorable' (movable by pleading) — no amount of begging will turn it aside.

words.definition: Prone to sudden, unpredictable shifts in mood or behavior.
words.example: The capricious manager praised the plan on Monday and scrapped it by Tuesday.
words.mnemonic: From Italian 'capra' (goat) — picture a capering goat leaping unpredictably this way and that.

words.definition: Changing moods quickly and unpredictably.
words.example: His mercurial temper could swing from laughter to fury within minutes.
words.mnemonic: Named for Mercury — the swift messenger god, and the metal that darts around when touched.

words.definition: Likely to change suddenly or turn dangerous without warning.
words.example: The stock market turned volatile, swinging wildly with every passing rumor.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'volare' (to fly) — volatile liquids fly off as vapor, ready to 'fly off the handle.'

words.definition: Able to change shape, role, or character with great ease.
words.example: The protean actor slipped from cackling villain to grieving father between two scenes.
words.mnemonic: From Proteus, the Greek sea god who kept changing shape to escape capture.

words.definition: A complete change of form, structure, or character in a living thing or situation.
words.example: Watching the caterpillar's metamorphosis, the class cheered when the wet-winged butterfly finally emerged.
words.mnemonic: Break it down: 'meta' (change) + 'morph' (form) — a change of form.

words.definition: To change one thing into another, especially into something of higher value.
words.example: Alchemists spent lifetimes trying to transmute dull lead into gleaming gold.
words.mnemonic: 'trans-' (across) + 'mute' (from mutare, to change) — mutate all the way across into something new.

words.definition: To change the outward appearance of something, often making it more beautiful or spiritual.
words.example: Dawn light poured in and transfigured the drab alley into something almost holy.
words.mnemonic: 'trans-' (change) + 'figure' — change the very figure or shape into a finer one.

words.definition: An unpredictable change or variation in one's circumstances or fortune over time.
words.example: Through every vicissitude of her long career, she carried the same battered notebook.
words.mnemonic: Say 'vi-SIS-i-tude' — picture a fickle sis (sister) whose moods and luck keep swinging.

words.definition: One of the possible ways a set of things can be ordered or arranged.
words.example: He gave up on the lock; there were far too many permutations to try by hand.
words.mnemonic: 'per' + 'mutation' — each mutation is one reshuffled ordering of the same pieces.

words.definition: A departure from the normal, usual, or expected, often a one-off lapse.
words.example: His outburst was an aberration; usually he's the calmest person in the room.
words.mnemonic: 'ab-' (away) + 'err' (to stray) — a straying away from the normal path.

words.definition: Something that differs from what is standard, normal, or expected.
words.example: The satellite flagged a heat anomaly right in the middle of the frozen lake.
words.mnemonic: Hear it as 'a-NOM-aly' → 'a not-normal-y' — a thing that just isn't normal.

words.definition: Not moving or flowing, and therefore stale, or showing no growth or activity.
words.example: Mosquitoes bred in the stagnant water pooled at the bottom of the abandoned pool.
words.mnemonic: Picture a 'stag' standing dead-still in a pond — from Latin 'stagnum', a still pool.

words.definition: Lacking the power to move or act; sluggish or chemically unreactive.
words.example: After the anesthetic wore off slowly, his arm still lay inert on the table.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'in a rut' — stuck, no get-up-and-go; 'in-' means 'not'.

words.definition: To establish something so firmly that it becomes very hard to change.
words.example: Decades of habit had entrenched the ritual so deeply that no one dared skip it.
words.mnemonic: Dig a 'trench' — soldiers dug into a trench are firmly set and hard to dislodge.

words.definition: To harden into bone, or to become rigid and resistant to change.
words.example: Over the years the committee's thinking ossified into a set of untouchable rules.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'os' (bone) + '-ify' (to make) — literally to turn into bone.

words.definition: To harden through mineral deposits, or to become fixed and unchanging.
words.example: His early curiosity had calcified into stubborn certainty by the time he turned fifty.
words.mnemonic: Think 'calcium' building up until soft tissue turns hard and chalky.

words.definition: To waste away or weaken, especially from lack of use or nourishment.
words.example: Months trapped in the cast left the muscles of his leg visibly atrophied.
words.mnemonic: 'a-' (without) + 'trophy' (from Greek 'trophe', nourishment) — without nourishment, it withers.

words.definition: To gradually decrease in size, strength, or intensity over time.
words.example: As the festival wore on, the crowd's energy began to wane and people drifted home.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'wain' — picture a wagon (an old 'wain') slowly rolling downhill, getting smaller as it fades from view.

words.definition: To gradually grow larger, stronger, or more intense over time.
words.example: As the moon began to wax, each night it appeared a little fuller than before.
words.mnemonic: Picture a candle building up as hot drips pile on and grow — 'wax' the noun becomes 'wax' the verb: it keeps growing.

words.definition: To gradually decline, recede, or fade away in strength or amount.
words.example: As the tide began to ebb, wet sand and stranded shells stretched further from the water.
words.mnemonic: 'Ebb' sounds like the deflating 'ehhh' of a balloon losing air — energy draining out and pulling back.

words.definition: To become steadily smaller in size, amount, or number.
words.example: Their savings dwindled after months without work, until only a few coins remained.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'wind'll' — wind blowing away a pile until little is left.

words.definition: To become less intense, severe, or forceful.
words.example: Only when the storm abated could the ferries finally leave the harbor.
words.mnemonic: A-BAIT: pull the bait off the hook and the fish's frenzy calms down.

words.definition: To sink to a lower level or grow calmer and quieter.
words.example: She waited for the swelling in her ankle to subside before trying to walk.
words.mnemonic: SUB-side → settling toward the underside, sinking down.

words.definition: To begin growing rapidly and thrive.
words.example: The startup burgeoned from three friends in a garage into a thousand-person company.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like a 'bursting garden' — buds popping open all over in spring.

words.definition: To multiply or spread quickly in great numbers.
words.example: Cheap knockoffs proliferated online until the market was flooded with them.
words.mnemonic: PRO-LIFE-erate → life multiplying fast, cells dividing again and again.

words.definition: To thrive, develop strongly, and be at one's healthiest or most successful.
words.example: Ferns flourished in the damp, shady corner where nothing else would take root.
words.mnemonic: Hidden 'flour' → well-fed plants and bakers alike thrive with plenty on hand.

words.definition: To dry up, shrivel, and lose vitality, as a plant starved of water.
words.example: Left unwatered for a week, the basil on the sill withered to brown stalks.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'weather' — plants left out in harsh weather shrivel and droop.

words.definition: To decline into a worse, lower, or less functional condition.
words.example: The polite debate degenerated into a shouting match within minutes.
words.mnemonic: DE-GENE-rate → moving away (de-) from a good origin (gene), breaking down.

words.definition: To become progressively worse in quality or condition.
words.example: His handwriting deteriorated as his hand tired near the end of the long exam.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'the tire ate' — the old tire ate itself away, getting worse daily.

words.definition: To wear away gradually through water, wind, or friction.
words.example: Years of crashing waves eroded the cliff until the lighthouse teetered at its edge.
words.mnemonic: E-RODE → water 'rode' over the rock again and again, wearing it down.

words.definition: To slowly eat away or destroy metal through chemical reaction such as rust.
words.example: Salt spray corroded the ship's bolts until they crumbled at a touch.
words.mnemonic: CORE-rode → acid riding into the core, rusting it from within.

words.definition: To rot or break down through natural decomposition.
words.example: The fallen apples decayed into the soil, drawing clouds of fruit flies.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a decade' — leave anything a decade and it rots away.

words.definition: To break apart completely into small fragments or pieces.
words.example: The ancient scroll disintegrated the moment he tried to unroll it.
words.mnemonic: DIS-INTEGRATE → the opposite of integrating; parts coming un-joined into bits.

words.definition: No longer in use because something newer or better has replaced it.
words.example: Floppy disks became obsolete once cheap USB drives arrived.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'ob-so-LATE' — so late to the party that nobody uses it anymore.

words.definition: Very old-fashioned and poorly suited to present-day needs or standards.
words.example: The office still ran on an antiquated filing system of paper index cards.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'antique' — as dated and dusty as an antique in a museum case.

words.definition: Close to ending or dying, and drained of energy and vitality.
words.example: After years of shrinking sales, the once-mighty firm was clearly moribund.
words.mnemonic: 'Mori' is Latin for death (as in mortuary) — a moribund thing is bound for the grave.

words.definition: No longer existing, operating, or working.
words.example: We found brochures from a travel agency that had shut its doors and gone defunct a decade ago.
words.mnemonic: 'De-' (not) + 'funct' (function) — it simply no longer functions.

words.definition: Just coming into being and starting to show signs of future growth.
words.example: The nascent startup had only three employees and a single rough prototype.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'natal' and 'native' (Latin 'nasci', to be born) — a nascent thing is newborn.

words.definition: At an early stage, just starting to appear or happen.
words.example: The doctor caught an incipient infection before any real symptoms showed.
words.mnemonic: Say 'in-SIP-ient' — you've taken only the first sip, so it has barely begun.

words.definition: At a very early, undeveloped stage that is not yet fully formed.
words.example: The plan is still embryonic — more a scribble on a napkin than a blueprint.
words.mnemonic: From 'embryo' — as tiny and unformed as an embryo in the womb.

words.definition: New, inexperienced, and only just getting started.
words.example: The fledgling airline owned just two planes and flew a single route.
words.mnemonic: A fledgling is a baby bird growing its first flight feathers — new and untested in the air.

words.definition: Only partly formed, vague, and not yet clearly worked out.
words.example: She had inchoate ideas for the novel but no plot or characters yet.
words.mnemonic: Say 'in-KO-ate' and picture 'in-cocoon' — still wrapped up and shapeless.

words.definition: To sprout and begin growing, the way a seed does.
words.example: The beans germinate within a week if the soil stays warm and damp.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'germ' — a seed's germ is the living part that bursts into growth.

words.definition: To develop gradually into a different or more complex form.
words.example: Her weekend hobby slowly evolved into a full-time business.
words.mnemonic: 'E-' (out) + 'volve' (roll) — to unroll gradually, like a scroll opening bit by bit.

words.definition: To adjust or change so as to fit new conditions.
words.example: Desert foxes have huge ears that help them adapt to the brutal heat.
words.mnemonic: 'Ad-' (to) + 'apt' (fitting) — to make yourself apt, or well-suited, to a situation.

words.definition: To make small changes to a text or law in order to improve it.
words.example: Congress voted to amend the bill by adding two new clauses.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'mend' — you mend a document by fixing its flaws.

words.definition: To look over something again and change it to correct or improve it.
words.example: After the editor's notes, he had to revise the third chapter twice.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-' (again) + 'vise' (see, as in 'vision') — to see it again and change what's there.

words.definition: To arrange, form, or present something in a new way.
words.example: The director recast the gloomy report as a story of hard-won progress.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-' (again) + 'cast' — to melt it down and pour it into a fresh mold.

words.definition: To completely change the shape, appearance, or nature of something.
words.example: A fresh coat of paint and new lights can transform a dull room into a cozy space.
words.mnemonic: TRANS- (across) + FORM: you carry a thing across into a whole new form.

words.definition: To give something a new and improved structure, look, or arrangement.
words.example: The company decided to revamp its outdated website with a cleaner layout and faster checkout.
words.mnemonic: RE- + VAMP: put a fresh 'vamp' (the front of a shoe) on an old boot to make it new again.

words.definition: To repair and restore an old building or structure to good condition.
words.example: They spent a year renovating the crumbling farmhouse, replacing the roof and rotten floors.
words.mnemonic: RE- (again) + NOV (new, as in 'novel'): make it new again.

words.definition: To make someone feel or look young, fresh, and full of energy again.
words.example: A week by the sea rejuvenated her, and she returned to work bursting with energy.
words.mnemonic: RE- + JUVEN (Latin 'juvenis' = young, like 'juvenile'): become young again.

words.definition: To bring new strength, activity, or vigor to something that has weakened.
words.example: New shops and a riverside park revitalized the once-empty downtown district.
words.mnemonic: RE- + VITAL (life): put the 'vital' life force back in.

words.definition: A fresh rise or return of something after a period of decline.
words.example: Vinyl records saw a surprising resurgence, with sales climbing every year for a decade.
words.mnemonic: RE- + SURGE: a wave that surges back up after pulling away.

words.definition: A revival of interest, activity, or achievement in art, culture, or a field.
words.example: The neighborhood is enjoying a culinary renaissance, with bold new restaurants opening monthly.
words.mnemonic: French for 'rebirth' — RE- + NAISS (born, like 'natal'): born anew.

words.definition: The natural regrowth or renewal of tissue, systems, or a damaged area.
words.example: A lizard's tail is capable of regeneration, growing back after it breaks off.
words.mnemonic: RE- + GENERATE: to generate (create) once more.

words.definition: A return to a worse state after a period of improvement, especially in illness.
words.example: The patient was recovering well until a sudden relapse sent her back to the hospital.
words.mnemonic: RE- + LAPSE: you lapse (slip) back down again.

words.definition: To go back to a previous condition, habit, or topic.
words.example: After the trial ended, the software would revert to its original locked settings.
words.mnemonic: RE- + VERT (turn, as in 'U-turn'): turn back to where you were.

words.definition: To move back, withdraw, or gradually grow fainter and more distant.
words.example: As the tide receded, a wide stretch of wet sand and stranded shells appeared.
words.mnemonic: RE- + CEDE (go, as in 'proceed'): go backward.

words.definition: To move backward to a less developed or worse condition.
words.example: Without daily practice, his piano skills began to regress to a beginner's level.
words.mnemonic: RE- + GRESS (step, like 'progress'): step backward instead of forward.

words.definition: A gradual slide into disorder, randomness, or breakdown within any system.
words.example: Left untended for years, the garden gave in to entropy, choked with weeds and fallen branches.
words.mnemonic: EN- + TROP (turning, Greek 'trope'): a system turning inward toward chaos.

words.definition: To cause something to continue or be preserved for a very long time.
words.example: Repeating the rumor only perpetuates a myth that scientists disproved decades ago.
words.mnemonic: PERPETU- (as in 'perpetual', never-ending): keep it going forever.

words.definition: To ensure someone or something is remembered forever, often through art or writing.
words.example: The poet immortalized the small fishing village in verses still read three centuries later.
words.mnemonic: IM- (not) + MORTAL (able to die): make it never die in memory.

words.definition: To place or protect an idea, right, or memory as cherished and permanent.
words.example: The right to a fair trial is enshrined in the constitution.
words.mnemonic: en- + SHRINE: you put something inside a shrine to honor and protect it forever.

words.definition: Impossible to erase, remove, or forget once it has been made.
words.example: The disaster left an indelible mark on everyone who lived through it.
words.mnemonic: in- (not) + 'delible' (think DELETE): it cannot be deleted.

words.definition: Deeply fixed in someone's nature and very hard to change.
words.example: Politeness was so ingrained in her that she thanked even the rudest clerk.
words.mnemonic: Worked into the GRAIN of the wood — soaked deep into the fibers, not just the surface.

words.definition: Having a long-established, firmly settled habit that is unlikely to change.
words.example: An inveterate gambler, he could not walk past a casino without going in.
words.mnemonic: 'veter-' as in VETERAN: a long-serving veteran of the habit, at it for years.

words.definition: Lasting a long time or constantly recurring, especially an illness or problem.
words.example: Her chronic back pain flared up every winter for a decade.
words.mnemonic: CHRONos, the Greek god of time — it drags on and on through time.

words.definition: Done regularly and repeatedly until it becomes second nature.
words.example: His habitual lateness eventually cost him the job.
words.mnemonic: You wear it like a monk's HABIT — the same robe pulled on every single day.

words.definition: Able to last a long time without breaking or wearing out.
words.example: These boots are durable enough to survive years of mountain hiking.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'durare', to last — the same root as ENDURE.

words.definition: Able to recover quickly from difficulty, shock, or damage.
words.example: After the flood, the resilient community rebuilt within a single year.
words.mnemonic: Like a rubber band that springs back — 'resile' literally means to spring back.

words.definition: Holding firmly to a purpose and refusing to give up.
words.example: Her tenacious pursuit of the story eventually exposed the whole scandal.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'tenere', to hold — a TENANT holds tight to the lease and won't let go.

words.definition: Stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course of action.
words.example: The obstinate child ate nothing but plain toast for an entire week.
words.mnemonic: OB-STANDS-in-the-way: it plants its feet in your path and won't move.

words.definition: Very hard to control, manage, or solve.
words.example: The negotiators finally gave up on the intractable border dispute.
words.mnemonic: in- (not) + 'tract' (to pull/handle): it gives no TRACTION, so you can't get a grip on it.

words.definition: Stubbornly resisting authority, control, or discipline.
words.example: The recalcitrant recruit ignored every order the sergeant barked.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'calcitrare', to kick with the heel — a recalcitrant mule kicks back against the reins.

words.definition: Stubbornly refusing to change, often without pity or remorse.
words.example: The judge remained obdurate despite the family's tearful pleas.
words.mnemonic: ob- + DURA (hard, as in 'dura mater'): hardened all the way through, heart and all.

words.definition: Unwilling to change or compromise; rigid in rules or attitude.
words.example: The airline's inflexible policy refused any refund, even for a hospital stay.
words.mnemonic: in- (not) + FLEXIBLE: it simply won't flex or bend, no matter the pressure.

words.definition: Firm and refusing to give way under pressure or persuasion.
words.example: The captain was unyielding, steering into the storm despite the crew's protests.
words.mnemonic: un- (not) + YIELDING: like a driver who ignores every YIELD sign and never slows.
